notes.text: The paper's argument is that digital wellbeing isn't really about using your phone less, it's about knowing how you actually use it. The gap between what you think you used and what the phone logged is the thing they care about, and WellScreen is a small tool built to show you that gap every day.
What's a probe? Not a finished app. It's a simple tool people use in real life for a short time so the researchers can learn from how they use it (they define it in section 3.1). WellScreen is one.

What's positive affect, and is 10% a lot? It's a questionnaire score (PANAS) of how many positive feelings you report. The median went from 29 to 34 out of 50 for the 20 people who finished, over two weeks (Table 7). So it's modest amount I would say.

Why the quotes around technology panics? Orben (reference no.65) showed that novels, radio, TV and games each set off a cycle of alarm that eventually faded. I think the authors are basically signalling they don't take the alarm at face value.

What does digital wellbeing even mean? It's a research area asking how people stay healthy and balanced when so much of life runs through screens. And it's not the same thing as "use your phone less" (which is kind of the whole point of the paper).

Who's Haidt? Jonathan Haidt, The Anxious Generation (2024), the best known version of "phones are wrecking teenagers." Odgers and others push back that the evidence is small and inconsistent. The paper sits more on the sceptical side.

If I remember one term from this paper it's this one. The E-A gap is the difference between how much you think you used your phone and what the phone actually logged. A negative gap means you guessed too low.
What's an RQ? A research question. These three are basically the promises the paper makes, and sections 4, 5 and 6 answer one each.

What did participants actually do? Every morning they guessed the day's phone use by app category, re-guessed yesterday, typed in the real numbers from their screen-time screen, looked at a chart comparing all three, answered a short survey, and wrote a line of reflection.
Is the stress finding really about self-awareness? or maybe just about being asked to predict every single morning?

What are SUS and IAM? Two standard questionnaires. SUS scores how usable something is (0 to 100, and 80 is good). IAM scores whether a tool feels right for its purpose (4 to 20, and 14 is kind of middling). They explain both in 6.1.1.
Why this number? It's the strongest evidence that timers and limits don't really work: people followed 2 in 100 of them. That's why they try awareness instead of restriction.

The prior tools they name: Rabbit Hole Tracker asks what you meant to do at each unlock, MyTime lets you set your own phone rules, Lock n' LoL locks a whole group's phones together, and One Sec adds a delay before an app opens. WellScreen is different because it asks you to predict instead of restricting you.
What are friction-based interactions? Small obstacles put there on purpose (a delay, an extra tap, a confirmation) to break an automatic habit.
What's co-design? Designing with the people who'll use the tool (workshops, sketching together) instead of designing for them and testing afterwards.
What's an IRB? A university ethics board that has to approve any study with human participants before it starts (consent, privacy, risks, payment).
Map of the app: Figure 1 on the next page shows the six screens in the order a participant sees them each morning, from login to the reflection survey.
Where did participants come from? Subreddits for specific universities. 91 people applied, 25 were picked for a mix of programs, and 20 finished. They got two 20 dollar gift cards.
Sampling: Reddit users at the authors' own universities who answered a flyer. Who's missing? People not on Reddit, and people avoiding screen-time tools on purpose (maybe the interesting ones?)
18 of 25 identify as Asian, and one participant is 50 to 65 in a college sample. Maybe P21 alone is driving the age coefficients in Tables 4 and 5?

What are these four scales? Standard psych questionnaires taken at entry and exit. BFI-10 is Big Five personality in ten questions, SSRQ is self-regulation (how well you manage goals), BSCS is self-control (resisting impulses), and PANAS-SF is positive and negative mood. They basically let the authors compare people on the same footing.

What's a covariate? A trait they measure so the analysis can separate its effect from the tool's effect. Like, is the gap smaller because of the app, or because that person is just naturally disciplined?
Where do the categories come from? The phone's own groupings (Screen Time on iOS, Digital Wellbeing on Android), so participants were only copying numbers they could already see on their phones.
Why type the numbers in by hand instead of just reading Screen Time directly? Maybe the chore of entering them is itself the reflection? or maybe the reason five people quit.
Attrition: 5 of the 25 dropped out, so most results are really about the 20 who finished. Only 9 logged 14 days in a row, the rest took about 16 days.

What's a t-test? Basically a statistics check for whether two numbers really differ, or whether the difference could just be chance. "Paired" means each person gets compared with themselves (their own guess against their own actual use), not with other people.
What's a mixed-effects model? A statistical model built for when the same person gives you 14 days of data. It separates differences between people from day to day changes within one person.

What's thematic analysis, and what are codes? Codes are short labels stuck on bits of interview text, like tagging a quote "felt guilty" or "phone before bed". Thematic analysis is grouping hundreds of those tags into a few bigger patterns (themes) that answer the research questions. Here two authors did the grouping, going from 1,068 codes down to 5 themes.
The headline result: people guessed too high on entertainment (by 11%) and too low on productivity (17%) and social apps (9%), but their overall totals were about right.

Why would students underestimate social use now when Facebook users in 2020 overestimated it? Maybe short-video autoplay? Maybe messaging apps getting counted as Social? The paper doesn't test either.

What does it mean that self-control was significant? People who scored higher on the self-control questionnaire guessed their use more accurately. Nothing else they measured (age, sex, phone type, personality) reliably predicted the gap.

The paper gives this as -1.3E-3 per minute of gap, which is really hard to picture. Worked out, a whole hour of misjudging your phone use moves daily satisfaction by less than a tenth of a point. So "linked with higher satisfaction" is true on paper, but I'd want effects like this reported in units I can actually feel and understand.

This was the result I found most interesting. Guessing accurately went with feeling satisfied and in control, but also with feeling more stressed and less able to keep to goals. Section 7.1.1 kind of wrestles with it.

How to read Table 4: each column is one app category, each row is something about the person (age, personality, self-control, and so on), and the number says how that thing moves the gap between guessed and actual minutes. A minus sign means more of that thing goes with a smaller gap, so more accurate guessing. A plus sign means a bigger gap. The stars mark the numbers that are unlikely to be chance, and most rows don't have any (self-control is the one that keeps showing up).

What's Cohen's d? It tells you how big a change is, not just whether there was one. It compares the average change to how much people normally differ from each other. Around 0.2 is small (you'd barely notice it), 0.5 is medium, and 0.8 is large (pretty obvious). Positive mood got 0.63, so a noticeable change, somewhere between medium and large. Mood got better, but self-control and self-regulation didn't.
The self-discrepancy explanation cuts both ways I would say.

What's self-discrepancy theory? Higgins (1989): distress comes from the gap between who you are and who you think you should be, and reflecting can shrink the gap you feel without changing what you do. That's how the authors explain mood getting better while habits stayed the same.
The finding everyone (me included) will recognise: the most common problem habit was the phone first thing in the morning and last thing at night, plus grabbing it whenever a conversation goes quiet.

Screen time can't tell the difference between using your phone to cope (getting away from a rough day) and using it out of mindless habit, since both just show up as minutes. If a tool treats all of it as "too much", it could end up shaming someone for coping, which could genuinely do harm. So I'd want a design that tells the two apart without asking the person every single time.
What's fidelity? How polished a prototype is. WellScreen was a rough web app that glitched, which probably dragged the usability score down, and it's part of why the authors call the study formative.

What's Figure 3 showing? The 20 finishers split by self-control and by how usable they found the app. People with low self-control who also found it usable were the keenest to keep using it, and where either was missing the enthusiasm dropped off.

This is why screen time is a flawed measure: music on Spotify with the screen off counts as nothing, the same music on YouTube with the screen on counts fully, and falling asleep with TikTok open counts all night.

The title quote, a participant defending their numbers in a daily log. The authors read this as the tool turning into a mirror people argue with, so reporting became judging and justifying instead of just measuring.
What's the observer effect? People change what they do because they know they're being watched. Some participants used their phones less just to beat their own morning guess.
Why can't they say the app caused anything? There was no comparison group, so stress could be causing accurate guessing instead of the other way around. The authors say this themselves.
The design tension here: the people who need it least find it a chore, and the person who needs it most (P9) felt sad looking at the numbers. So who's the target user?

Policy angle: if a school or employer rolled out a tool like this, it could feel pointless to disciplined people and punishing to everyone else. The authors warn against tying it to performance reviews.
The design takeaway: the value was in pausing to guess and then checking, not in being accurate. A future app could do this with one morning prompt and one evening prompt.
Where AI comes in: letting people ask questions about their own data in plain language, and having the app ask them questions back. They frame it as a conversation partner and a game, not a judge.
A companion that asks whether a spike was on purpose is really a prompt design problem, which is pretty much what we're doing in 711 studio.

Limitations: two weeks, 25 US students, no comparison group, a glitchy prototype, novelty and observer effects, and screen time as a pretty crude proxy. So I'd read the findings as promising, not proven.
